title: September | 2026 | FRED Blog
gist: A FRED Blog post shows US consumer sentiment (Michigan index, 95.9 average in 2019 vs 71.7 in January 2025) collapsed post-pandemic while the SHED share of adults saying they are 'at least doing okay financially' barely moved (75% in 2019 vs 73% in 2025) — but a second SHED question, 'worse off than 12 months ago,' tracks the sentiment collapse closely. The gap is framed as levels-versus-change, rising dispersion across households, and own-finances-versus-broad-economy.

insights.claim: The University of Michigan Index of Consumer Sentiment averaged 95.9 in 2019 and stood at 71.7 in January 2025, a roughly 24-point drop that has not reversed.
insights.speaker: St. Louis Fed — FRED Blog
insights.so_what: Anchors how far sentiment-driven demand signals sit below pre-COVID norms; a mean-reversion trade in consumer-facing names needs a catalyst this gap has not yet produced.
insights.quote: Its value averaged 95.9 in 2019 and was 71.7 in January 2025.
insights.locator: Are you doing OK? — 'Before the COVID-19 pandemic, these two measures moved'

insights.claim: The share of US adults reporting they are 'at least doing okay financially' in the Federal Reserve Board's SHED survey was 75% in 2019 and 73% in 2025, essentially flat despite the collapse in headline consumer sentiment.
insights.speaker: St. Louis Fed — FRED Blog
entities: Survey of Household Economics and Decisionmaking
insights.so_what: Self-reported household balance-sheet health held up even as survey mood cratered — a reason to weight spending data over sentiment surveys when sizing consumer exposure.
insights.quote: It was 75% in 2019 and it was 73% in 2025.
insights.locator: Are you doing OK? — 'The share of adults saying they're doing at least okay'

insights.claim: Measures of household financial well-being and measures of consumer sentiment moved together before COVID-19 but decoupled afterward, so the historical correlation between the two can no longer be assumed.
insights.speaker: St. Louis Fed — FRED Blog
insights.so_what: Models that map sentiment onto household financial condition need re-estimation on post-2020 data or they will overstate consumer distress.
insights.quote: Measures of household financial well-being don’t always align with consumer sentiment. You can feel relatively secure about your finances while still being pessimistic about the overall economy.

insights.claim: A second SHED question — whether households are worse off financially than 12 months ago — dropped sharply after the pandemic and has stayed low, matching the trajectory of consumer sentiment rather than diverging from it.
insights.speaker: St. Louis Fed — FRED Blog
insights.so_what: Choosing which SHED series to cite flips the conclusion about the consumer entirely; check which question underlies any 'households are fine' claim.
insights.locator: Are you worse off today? — 'Here, the two measures tell a more similar story.'

insights.claim: The divergence between the two SHED series is explained partly as a levels-versus-change distinction: 'doing okay financially' describes a current position while 'worse off than a year ago' describes the direction of travel, and a household can report both simultaneously.
insights.speaker: St. Louis Fed — FRED Blog
insights.so_what: A reusable lens for reading any survey: solvency questions and momentum questions are separate signals, and momentum is what tracks mood and voting behavior.
insights.quote: Saying you’re doing okay financially describes your current financial position. Saying you’re worse off than a year ago describes how that position has changed.

insights.claim: Consumer sentiment appears to track the perceived change in household finances more closely than the perceived level of them, implying sentiment recovers only when households feel better than a year prior, not when they merely feel solvent.
insights.speaker: St. Louis Fed — FRED Blog
insights.so_what: Sets the bar for a sentiment rebound: needs a visible year-over-year improvement in real household finances, not just stabilization.
insights.locator: Measured this way, households' assessments of their own finances

insights.claim: The gap between the two SHED measures may reflect financial experiences becoming more uneven across US households, with some doing relatively well while others deteriorate — an inequality story hidden inside stable aggregate averages.
insights.speaker: St. Louis Fed — FRED Blog
insights.so_what: Supports a barbell read of consumer demand — premium and value formats gaining at the expense of the middle — rather than a uniform 'consumer is fine' call.
insights.quote: It’s also possible that financial experiences have become more uneven across households, with some households doing relatively well while others have seen their financial situations deteriorate

insights.claim: A stable aggregate share of adults 'doing okay financially' is compatible with widening dispersion underneath, so the headline percentage alone cannot distinguish broad stability from offsetting improvement and deterioration.
insights.speaker: St. Louis Fed — FRED Blog
insights.so_what: Treat flat aggregate wellbeing prints as uninformative about distribution; demand the by-income cuts before concluding the consumer is healthy.
insights.locator: consistent with the divergence of the two SHED measures

insights.claim: The Michigan consumer sentiment index is broader than the SHED wellbeing question because it incorporates views about personal finances, business conditions, and buying conditions, leaving room for people to feel personally secure while judging the economy harshly.
insights.speaker: St. Louis Fed — FRED Blog
insights.so_what: Much of the sentiment shortfall may be about perceived macro and price conditions rather than household finances — read it as a signal on policy and pricing perception, not spending capacity.

insights.claim: The FRED Blog explicitly declines to attribute the sentiment-wellbeing divergence to any single cause, presenting three candidate explanations while stating the graphs do not identify the driver.
insights.speaker: St. Louis Fed — FRED Blog
insights.so_what: Anyone citing this Fed material as proof that sentiment is 'wrong' or that households are fine is overreaching the source.
insights.quote: The graphs don’t tell us exactly what’s driving the difference
insights.locator: The graphs don't tell us exactly what's driving the difference

insights.claim: The SHED wellbeing series are annual and thinly historied — the 'at least doing okay' series runs from 2013 to 2025 and the 'worse off than 12 months ago' series from 2014 to 2025 — so both comparisons rest on roughly a dozen annual observations.
insights.speaker: St. Louis Fed — FRED Blog
insights.so_what: Low sample depth caps how much statistical weight the divergence can bear; treat it as a stylized fact, not an estimated relationship.

insights.claim: The St. Louis Fed's recent published blog output clusters on AI's labor-market effects — including whether generative AI saves time at work and whether AI is reducing employment for software coders — alongside rent affordability and state and metro employment.
insights.speaker: St. Louis Fed — FRED Blog
insights.so_what: A regional Fed devoting recurring research bandwidth to AI displacement is an early tell that AI labor substitution is entering the official policy-data conversation.
